The quality of random allocation concealment in randomized controlled trials (RCTs) is assessed as follows: a score of 2 indicates adequate concealment of allocation, 1 indicates uncertainty or lack of description, and 0 indicates inadequate concealment or quasi-randomization. 2. The comparability of groups at baseline is evaluated as follows: a score of 2 indicates comparable groups, 1 indicates that comparability is not mentioned, and 0 indicates that the groups are not comparable. 3. The blinding of healthcare providers is scored as follows: 2 if blinding is explicitly stated, 1 if it is not mentioned or unclear, and 0 if blinding is not performed. 4. The blinding of outcome assessors to the intervention is scored as follows: 2 if blinding is explicitly stated, 1 if it is not mentioned or unclear, and 0 if blinding is not performed. 5. The follow-up time is scored as follows: 2 for follow-up periods exceeding one year, 1 for follow-up periods less than one year, and 0 if no follow-up is conducted (assessment only at the end of the trial). 6. The percentage of follow-up at the end of the trial or follow-up period is scored as follows: 2 for 60% or more, 1 for 40-59%, and 0 for less than 40%. 7. Details of dropouts are scored as follows: 2 if the number and reasons for withdrawals are stated, 1 if only withdrawals are mentioned without numbers or reasons, and 0 if not mentioned. 8. The use of validated outcome measures is scored as follows: 2 for validated measures, 1 if unclear, and 0 if not used. 9. The reporting of outcomes is scored as follows: 2 if outcomes are measured objectively, 1 if self-reported, and 0 if not stated. 10. Intention-to-treat analysis is scored as follows: 2 if performed, 1 if possibly performed but unclear, and 0 if not performed. 11. The total score for the quality of an RCT is calculated out of 20. A score greater than 15 indicates strong quality, 10-15 indicates moderate quality, and less than 10 indicates weak quality. 12. The Shuring RP 2009 study was a double-blind cluster RCT aimed at evaluating the combined protective effect of BCG vaccination and rifampicin in preventing leprosy among contacts of leprosy patients. 13. In the COLEP trial, eligible contacts of leprosy patients were administered either a single dose of 600 mg rifampicin or a placebo under supervision. BCG vaccination was provided at birth as per WHO recommendations. 14. The follow-up period for the study was four years, with two follow-up assessments conducted. The dropout rate and details of losses to follow-up were described. 15. The research question and objectives of the study were clearly stated, and the study population was well-defined. The participation rate of eligible individuals was at least 50%. 16. The study ensured that all subjects were selected or recruited from similar populations during the same time period, with uniform application of inclusion and exclusion criteria. 17. A justification for the sample size, including power calculations and effect estimates, was provided. 18. The exposure of interest was measured prior to the outcome assessment, and the timeframe was sufficient to observe an association between exposure and outcome if it existed. 19. The exposure measures were clearly defined, valid, reliable, and consistently implemented across all participants. The exposure was assessed more than once over time. 20. The outcome measures were clearly defined, valid, reliable, and consistently implemented across all participants. Outcome assessors were blinded to the exposure status of participants. 21. Loss to follow-up after baseline was 20% or less, and key potential confounding variables were measured and statistically adjusted for their impact on the exposure-outcome relationship. 22. The study reviewed evidence on the effectiveness of vaccines for leprosy prevention, including BCG, ICRC, and Mycobacterium w vaccines, under programmatic conditions with or without chemoprophylaxis. 23. Evidence from systematic reviews and individual studies until 2010 was analyzed, including the protective effects of BCG vaccination and its combination with other interventions. 24. The BCG vaccine demonstrated varying levels of protective efficacy against leprosy, with evidence from experimental and observational studies. However, heterogeneity among studies and potential overestimation of effects in observational studies were noted. 25. The ICRC vaccine and Mycobacterium w vaccine showed moderate-quality evidence of protective effects against leprosy in RCTs, with significant reductions in incidence compared to placebo. 26. The MALTALEP study protocol, published in 2013, aims to evaluate the combined preventive effects of single-dose rifampicin and BCG vaccination among contacts of newly diagnosed leprosy patients in Bangladesh. 27. The study design is a cluster RCT with two treatment arms: BCG alone and BCG combined with rifampicin. Approximately 1,300 patients and 20,000 contacts will be enrolled, with random allocation to treatment arms. 28. Inclusion criteria include household contacts, those living in the same compound, and first neighbors. Exclusion criteria include refusal of consent, pregnancy, current TB or leprosy treatment, age under five years, liver disease, temporary residence, and contact with another patient. 29. The primary outcome is the number of new leprosy cases emerging from contact groups. Blood samples will be collected for immune and gene profiling. 30. The study will contribute to understanding the effectiveness of combined chemoprophylaxis and immunoprophylaxis in leprosy prevention under programmatic conditions.
